utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Registrar, will you please have the accused brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, of course, I should like to see whether the interpreters can hear me, if everybody is ready. I see that both counsel for the Prosecution and Defence are here. The accused has also arrived. Shall we now have the protected witness introduced, and I give the floor to Mr. Nice for the Prosecution to beg and to introduce his witness. If I'm correct, it is Witness N [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "M" or "N"? "M," I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, because I have two documents here. I believe it is "M."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness M, I am talking to you. Will you please sit down? Do not stand up.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, I believe that the witness can stand up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. If you hear me, will you please stand up for a few moments? First, you will check on a piece of paper, on a document. You will now see whether this is your name, but do not pronounce it; just indicate whether it is your name or not. Is it your name? Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you will make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated now. The Tribunal thank you for coming here at the request of the Prosecutor in order to testify in the trial conducted by the International Tribunal against accused, Mr. Goran Jelisic, who is sitting to your left. Let me explain to you. First you will hear the questions of the Prosecution; then of the Defence; and then the Judges, if they wish so, will also ask you some questions at the end of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. You will tell us what you have to say. Of course, it is very difficult, but be calm. If you need a break, please tell us and we shall make a break for a few minutes. Mr. Nice, the floor is yours. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness M, have you considered a summary of your evidence, the first summary which was, I think, distributed to the Defence, having to be amended as to one paragraph, paragraph 6, and have you recently, very recently, gone over that amended summary in English, having it read over to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can hand the witness a copy of the amended version in English and the language he understands. The Chamber already has, I think, the amended versions before it. May he look at it and acknowledge it as his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When that was read over to you today, subject to the one correction that appears in the revised paragraph 6, was it accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I now see that I should like to make yet another correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It is paragraph 1: "After the explosion of the Sava bridge, the witness saw a body ..." Not a body but parts of a number of bodies, more than one body lying in the street, under the bridge, and on the roofs of the surrounding buildings where tiles had not yet flown off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: There is also the damage. There is also the damage. There was a major material damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the witness otherwise then acknowledging the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness M, you can leave the statement on one side. You don't have to follow it. It's probably better if you simply face the Judges and answer the questions that I shall ask you. Just dealing with paragraph 1, after the explosions and seeing the body parts on the street and observing the damage, did you, a couple of hours later, go to work at the Bimal factory, there being soldiers there who effectively occupied the factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, at the same time, although it's not in your summary, but I think there's quite a tall tower nearby. Did you notice something about what the state of fortification of that tower was at this early hour of the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it you noticed on top of the tower?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I noticed that there were more than two soldiers on that silo, and that was the highest point in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they have by way of armaments, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go up to see, but I realised that they had heavy machine gun with them and they also had their personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having been sent home by the soldiers at the Bimal factory -- and I think the Bimal factory manufactures oil. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, it makes oil. It's not soldiers who sent me home; it was my manager who told me it would be best for me to go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then rounded up a couple of days later, on the 3rd or 4th of May, by Serb soldiers and taken to what is described in the summary as a clinic? Was that a medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, to be precise, in the afternoon, around 1.00 or half past one or perhaps 2.00, whatever the case, they took us all. Mauzer was using a loudspeaker, calling to people, telling them to come out of their homes, to raise their hands like this [indicates] and to move towards the health centre, towards the emergency care.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If asked by the Judges or by Defence counsel, can you give a detail of the treatment at the health clinic? I'm not going to ask you for that detail.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man Mauzer, did he seem to be generally in charge of the operation of rounding people up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one incident, and again it's not in the summary but you might just help us with this. At the emergency unit, did you see somebody writing names on a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the assistance of my friend, this is at the foot of the statement of the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, page 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see somebody writing some names down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it who was doing the writing, why was he writing, and what was he writing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: (redacted). But when they saw that he had a Muslim last name, they began to tease him and to beat him, and when he was scared out of his wits, they felt it and told him to write down the names of all the extremists in the hallway of the emergency unit, and he was doing it when I saw him there. He was sitting, straddling a bench in the health centre. He was writing down some names. At some point, I managed to come close enough to tell him not to make a mistake, just to forget that my name exists, because they might kill me if he put me on that list, because I had already seen some names there, even though I can't remember which ones they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he writing this list happily and by agreement, or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It wasn't agreement or his will; it was fear. One could read it in his eyes. And tears were running down his face and his legs were shaking as if he was on hot coals. His lips were all swollen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the health centre or clinic, having been searched and so on, were you taken to the mosque, there being already some five or six hundred men at the mosque when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken back to the clinic for interrogation about your background and political associations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that place -- and I needn't ask you to deal with this in detail because the Chamber has heard quite a lot about this already, but at that place did you see the man named Papa being dealt with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see other atrocious acts committed while you were there which you can give detail of, if anybody wants to know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can, if anybody wishes to know. Now, the question is, of course, if there is anyone who wishes to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, yourself, beaten or ill-treated in any way in the course of your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom and how badly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: In the health centre, I wasn't beaten too badly, but I was kicked and punched. For about two minutes, a pistol was put into my mouth and a knife under my throat, and I was pushed off the chair until some captain or, rather, somebody who they called the captain, came and stopped that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you finally taken to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: From the mosque, I was transferred with three minor children: with a Palestinian, and a minor whose brother was killed in the mosque when he tried to escape through the window, and with another young boy. I was taken to the barracks, to withstand first aid really, because I had trouble with my back. In the health centre they didn't have the kind of injection that I needed, so they took me to the barracks. They extended the first aid to me and I stayed there until May the 8th; that is, I was transferred from the mosque on the 6th, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You therefore arrived at Luka on what date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: On the 8th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there, did you go into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: We were brought by buses which were full; as many seats, as many prisoners. We had to keep our hands above our head. I already showed you. I can't lift my right hand because it was injured in the Batkovic camp. We had to keep our heads between our knees, practically, so as not to see where we were being taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on arrival, did you go into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. We were getting off the bus, one by one, and they had cocked rifles aimed at us, and one by one we were entering the hangar in which there were already people. I should say there must have been around 300 of them. It was the first hangar to the left-hand side as you enter Luka from the side where the petrol station is to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody introduce himself to the people in the hangar? If so, what did he say was his name? And tell us, more particularly, what he said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic entered and introduced himself as the Serb Adolf and said that nobody should be afraid unless he was an extremist, because they wanted to cleanse the Serbs of the extremist Muslims and balijas like one cleans the head of lice. That was something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what would happen to those who were not extremists and what processes would be applied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: What he said was quite enough, because he then turned on his heels and went out. After him, two girls, young women, came in and looked at us significantly and, I think, with quite a sardonic look in their eyes and went out, and some of them even laughed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the girls who were with Jelisic or who came in after he had been there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of any one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Later on, I heard that one of them was called Monika, but I did not know her personally. I only knew her by sight. She was quite a number of years younger than I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just back to your account of what Jelisic said, did he say what would happen to those who weren't extremists? Would they be allowed out? Just explain that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: We saw -- as we were going into the hangar, we could already see executions, and one knows what happens to those who need to be cleansed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you saw executions. At whose hands were people being executed when you went in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: A guy in a police uniform, I mean of the Yugoslav police, and with a huge baton some metre and a half long, perhaps even longer, he was taking, one by one, or sometimes two at a time, of inmates, and took them opposite to the office which I could see from the corner in which I was sitting in the hangar, because a door was left open enough to be able to have a good view of the situation outside, even though we had to avoid to be seen that we were looking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that stage, were you able to identify the man in the police uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I did not know him personally, but he looked like any other man; I mean quite normal, except there was some particular glean in his eyes. And he was brandishing this baton and saying, "Where are those extremists, where are those Green Berets?" When he took away brothers Zahirovic and came back when Goran Jelisic had finished them off, he said, "Well, now you see how extremists and Green Berets fare, and those who are neither of that have no reason to be afraid."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw the policemen taking men out, and did you see what happened to the men generally when they were taken out, before we come to the brothers Zahirovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Somebody, one of the Zahirovic brothers, was hit with the baton in the back and head two or three times as they were entering that other room; and another one, with practically his head split up, had come out of that office, and he merely finished him off with one or two bullets or -- I don't know. It depends on how many bullets he deemed necessary to fire into the victim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I must be just a little more detailed here. Dealing with the two brothers Zahirovic, were these the two taken out by a policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they taken first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: To the small room across. To an office. I believe it was an Intersped office where I was subsequently interrogated and where I saw a lot of bloodstains on the walls and furniture and bookshelf, and I even saw a thatch of hair, presumably torn off with the skin of the head and just stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were the brothers in that room before they came out again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I'm not a hundred per cent sure, but I do not think that it was more than five or ten minutes. Perhaps even that is too long, because everything was taking place with such speed, or perhaps it seemed to us that way. We were so afraid that I really couldn't focus all that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. If the witness could initially just have Exhibit number 9, please. Then I'll hand another exhibit in to the usher which will become whatever the latest exhibit number is. First number 9.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 44.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you'd look first at existing Exhibit 9. If you use the pointer you'll be provided with, staying in your seat, just to remind the Judges of the geography, can you just point out where you went to in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Shall I show it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, just point. If you use the pointer and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I don't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not coming up on the ELMO. There it is. Can you just point out where the hangar was to which that you went, and where was the office --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the office to which the men were taken and where you went for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The white building at the top of the three.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I've got nothing on my monitor, and I can't see over the top of the monitor to where he's pointing, I'm afraid. I've got absolutely nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have a similar problem over here. We get an intermittent picture only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that the Judges are the only ones who are privileged, but that is only natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video booth is asking whether Mr. Greaves could use another monitor -- that is, the one in front of Mr. Londrovic -- perhaps, because this particular screen seems to be out of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you could change places. Mr. Greaves, you will be conducting the cross-examination. If that is so, then perhaps you should change places with Mr. Londrovic. How about you, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If I can stand whilst he's doing this, I can actually see the ELMO. I can't see it if I'm sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. Very well, but you can move closer. You can move to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just point out again, please, the hangar and the office.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: [Indicates]. This is the hangar. This is where the entrance to the hangar was, and I was around here, around there [indicates]. I had a good view through the doors, which were open sufficiently so that I could see all this portion here [indicates], and this is where Jasce was, around here [indicates], at the kurb. This is where the grate was where the killings took place, and this is where the bodies were piled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Now can he now have a look at the next, Exhibit 44, which is taken at a later date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness M, that shows, I think, the entrance to the office that you're speaking of. If we can move it a little to the right so we can see the grate. Does this or does this not show the grate that you're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is the grate [indicates], but you cannot see it on the monitor right now. That's the one. This is the office [indicates]. It was probably demolished after the camp was dissolved, so that any trace or any evidence would be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the first brother Zahirovic went in for interrogation and whatever number of minutes passed, did he come out of the office and go the few steps between the office door and the grate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I believe that it was Zahirovic who first arrived. He had been beaten, and his head had been split open, and he was dragged over here. I cannot recall all the details because it was like horror movies which were playing out in front of those who were there. It was even dangerous to look because then you would be a potential next victim. So it is difficult. It was who came with his head broken from the baton and who with broken arms or ribs, but it was so Jelisic, whoever it was -- Jelisic killed him with a single bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the man's head at the time he shot him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Near the grate, but I'm not sure whether it was at the grate itself or about half a metre away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I was about 10 to 15 metres away from that spot, so I cannot tell with precision, but he was around the grate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second brother Zahirovic, is what happened to him the same or similar as that which happened to the first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who shot him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: In the same way, but it seems to me that one of the two brothers Zahirovic only got one bullet in the back of the head and the other one got two, and I cannot say which one. But later on, those of us who eyewitnessed this later commented, and we thought that it was so callous that he could kill people just like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jasmin Cumurovic, called Jasce, what you can tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: At that time, he remained at somewhere around the door to this office after being examined. It seems to me as if he had been ordered to wait there. He waited there for quite awhile, and he seemed as if he wasn't allowed to move while they were going around beating. Horrible sounds came out of that room. It was a small room, three by three or three by four metres. But everybody was in great fear. Very unusual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Cumurovic. Cumurovic had already been in for an interrogation; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: That I do not know, because I saw those two brothers, the Zahirovic brothers, when they were brought out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Cumurovic after the brothers had been shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic came from over here and went first towards the door. I think he must have taken a bottle of beer. Then he crossed the alley and came to Jasce and said -- asked him to smell his hand. I couldn't quite hear what he was saying. He wanted to -- but I know this gesture. Then he asked him to lick it. As he did, he fired one or two bullets into his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the correction I think you wanted to make as who did what, Cumurovic having been asked to lick his hand. What did Cumurovic do when he was given that instruction to lick this man's hand? Did he obey?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: This is what I was just talking about. When Goran Jelisic approached him, in his hand he had a Scorpion with a silencer, and it was the right or maybe the left hand in which he held the pistol. He put it in front of him so that he would lick it, and then about 10, 15 seconds, I guess, had to lick the blood. There was also a glove there with cut-off fingers. This must have been the blood that splattered when one of the two Zahirovic brothers was killed, apparently. Some blood had splattered on to the hand. Then presumably he asked him to lick off some of that blood or something. I don't know. As he bent over, he shot him in the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you later taken for interrogation yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: After Ramiz, whose last name I don't know. I know his nickname and I know where he worked. He worked in the electric utility company in Brcko. After that, Senad Poljo, (redacted), was taken away with Ranko Cesic. When he came for him, he cocked a rifle, he loaded it, and then he said, "Go on. Move." Five or six minutes later it was my turn. I don't know how long it took. It was five or six minutes. But I know when he came to get me, he looked around and he told me, "Get up. It's your turn now." Then he again cocked the rifle, trained it on me, and then he made me cross that way and follow him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who conducted the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It was -- there was a fat man from Bjeljina. Some of the camp inmates later told me where he was from. He was rather heavy. He had a round face and camouflage uniform. He looked too -- he was young but he looked older. He had a piece of paper and a pencil in front of him, and there was another one across from him meant for the person who was going to be interrogated. He asked me who I was, where I worked. While I was being interviewed, Goran Jelisic came in and hit Senad Poljo with the butt of his pistol against the temple and he fell off the chair. He had already had his head bandaged because he had been beaten previously. Senad started moaning and told Goran, "I'm not guilty of anything. I said everything. Ask him." "Ask him," meaning me, (redacted). Goran turned to me and said, "Do you know him?" I said, "Yes. (redacted)." He said, "Do you guarantee for him?" and I said, "I do." Then he said, "Give the two of them passes." The fat one was obviously not very happy. He said he hadn't finished with me. Then he said that -- Goran said that he should finish with us. I thought that this was the end, that it meant execution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, in fact, were the two of you given passes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, we were, but because we did not have documents which had been taken away from us when we entered the hangar, then the fat one, if I may call him so, asked me what my personal identity card number was. I told him that I didn't have it on me, that I only had my driver's licence on me. Goran said that they should go and find my driver's licence and Senad's personal identity card. I thought that this was just to sort of put me at ease and that what would follow would be a bullet in the back of the head. Then Goran left with Ranko Cesic somewhere in a car, and then this other man went to get the documents and really came back with them, which surprised me. He brought my driver's licence and Senad's personal identity card. He said, "Here." In fact, he called the fat one by his nickname, which I have forgotten. While he was writing down my personal citizen registration number which was on the driver's licence, he said that I should thank Mile and Goran. I said -- thanked him, but he said, "If it were up to me, you would have been swimming in Sava with your head down and stomach wide open." At this I started shaking uncontrollably and I was overcome by panic, because, one, I didn't know what to think anymore, because one of them was releasing me and the other one was killing me. So I didn't know what was going on. Then I was told that we could leave and I waited --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stop [inaudible]. While you were being spoken to by Jelisic, did Ranko come in and say something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Ranko came in and said -- this is before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Before Goran addressed me, he said, "Beat up these two well, because they know everything." Then he just turned and left. I think that Goran probably remembers that. He could confirm it. As we were leaving this small room, in the room where we were to be beaten and perhaps killed, which I assume was the wish of the person who was going to be -- who was going to interrogate me -- but I just forgot something. When we came to Mile, the stonemason, he asked me where I had been the last three months. I said that I had been working and that I was spending most of the time with (redacted) and that we were inseparable, like brothers. This is probably how Goran Jelisic knew me. I was too afraid to even look at him, so I didn't even recognise him. But this moment I will never forget. It was -- even today it sometimes appears in my dreams. He says --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I was asking you was did Ranko come in and tell Goran anything about what he, Ranko, had been doing at any stage of the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ranko come into the office at any stage and say to Goran something about what he had been doing or was doing; he, Ranko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Ranko, as I said, at one point entered and said only that Senad and I should be beaten up well because we knew everything, and he then left. I only saw him carrying a crate of beer with Goran Jelisic. And Goran Jelisic, as we were leaving, said, "Take a beer," which I did not do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be quite clear, do you have any recollection of Ranko saying anything about his having been doing some shooting; he, Ranko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My apologies. I'm too excited as I'm recalling all this. He called him outside to show him how he can -- how this rifle is a good rifle. He was shooting pigeons. Then he, that day, gave me this pass for life, as they called it. And then on the way out, they offered me some beer from this crate which they were carrying. I'm grateful to you, sir, for being reminded of this, because I tried not to bring back all these memories. But still, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you left Luka, did you see the movement of dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: During my stay there on the 8th of May, my neighbour, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: (redacted) -- he took his brother to this heap behind the building. When he came back, he was shaking, and he said, "I just put my brother on that heap. If at least I could have buried him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see other bodies being moved? Just "Yes" or "No" will do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed, in theory, to look at the movement of bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I heard an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say "No"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like to take a break, Witness M? I see that you're very shaken by these reminiscences. Would you like a break of a few minutes? Mr. Nice, are you going to go through the whole list? What are you planning to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm intending to summarise the rest of the witness's evidence, and as to the list, as I've already explained to Mr. Greaves, I'm going to deal with them in another way, because they are particularly distressing for the witness. The way I was going to deal with them would take a very short space of time indeed. So it might be prudent to try to get to the end of his examination-in-chief straightaway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, yes. But Witness M, the Judges do understand that you're now talking about horrible things that you experienced. Would you like a five-minute break, and the Victims and Witnesses Unit will take care of you? Would you like a break of five minutes to recover, or do you prefer to continue and have it done with? It is up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer to deal with it in one go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to summarise the position until this stage, Witness M, had you -- just running through the events very quickly, at the clinic, had you seen beatings; "Yes" or "No"? In the first place when you went to the clinic, had you seen beatings; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, and I can also tell you the number of people who were beaten up --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: -- before my very eyes, and probably there were additional ones who were beaten after I wasn't present anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen killings at the clinic, "Yes" or "No", actual killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you, at any time in the clinic, seen or found bodies; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, but I only saw several dead, actually -- for instance, I saw some legs. A door couldn't quite be closed. I guess the body had been dragged, and there was a trail of blood. Then in the basement there was also a pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the mosque there may have been two men killed in the course of an attempted escape, but apart from that, did you see any other actual killings at the mosque; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Apart from that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see beatings at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Luka, you saw and you've described Jelisic killing three men. Did you see any other killings yourself, "Yes" or "No", actually see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to say roughly. I'd like to say the exact number, which would be guesswork.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see doing the killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic, alias Serbian Adolf. I want to point out that I did not know his name, his real name. When I was exchanged, I became convinced that this was his real name and last name, because at the camp, I didn't fully believe that because a lot of them gave false names, and we didn't dare talk much about that in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These other killings, were they before or after the killings of the Zahirovic brothers? Or can't you say when they were; you can simply say that they happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I am sure that the Zahirovic brothers' murders were the first ones, because I arrived there in the afternoon. I was there until about 9.00. Actually, we were released at 8.30 because the curfew was at 9.00, so we only had 30 minutes to reach this neighbourhood which was about 1,5 kilometres from there. I apologise for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... that followed the Zahirovic and the Cumurovic killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Brothers Zahirovic, yes. Sorry. After Cumurovic's murder, was it -- yes, yes, it's quite all right. I'm sorry. I'm sorry about this. Yes, it's quite all right, yes. That is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... similar to the killings of the brothers Zahirovic, or were they different in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I heard a word which was used and which I remember leaving a tremendous impression on me and frightening me. I know you are Europeans and you know what the term "selective murder" means, but they used a word which meant all but one -- I can't remember that particular word, even though it did stick in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the meaning of this word that was used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I just told you: selective selection. It means a choice, and what you've selected, you can either drown or leave it on the surface.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can answer these questions, if I can suggest it to you, you can answer them "Yes" or "No". With your pass, provided in the way you described, were you able to return from the camp initially to the communities -- at the Es community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were there, did you see Jelisic on one occasion with a girl when he offered you a drink?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you returned to camp on a later date? Were you returned to the Luka camp eventually on a later date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: With those from Brezovo Polje, with people from the village to which I went into circumstances and where I stayed, because that was practically an open camp, an open prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went back to the camp in whatever it was, July, did you see anything of Jelisic there or did you not see anything of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I never saw him again, because after the 15th of May that I learned that, and those selective murders stopped, orders had come to take care of us so that we could be used for the exchange of prisoners, dead, and such like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at, but without going through in detail, two lists which will become Exhibit 45, and I want you simply to confirm, when they are before you -- so that the Judges can understand how we're going to deal with this, yes, both at the same time -- did you, at the request of the Prosecution, go through these lists, marking the names of those you recognised as people who, to your understanding, have been killed in the course of this overall conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I am choosing my words, but it is quite true that you are using that term "people". But it was only civilians who perished, and I think you should put it down on record, because you are not talking about civilians, you're not referring to civilians. Some people thought us to be, as I already said that -- I'm sorry, I'm sorry. My brain went blank for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry. All I'm going to ask you to do is to simply look at this exhibit, which is the two lists, and simply to tell us if this is the list marked either by you or in your presence with ticks and one or two other little bits of writing to indicate those civilian men who you knew and who, to your understanding, were killed. Just quickly look at the list and tell me if what I've suggested is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, that is the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the other list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we should take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the last question. All right, if it is the last one. If not, then we shall take a break. This is the last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think he understood that this is the list he marked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I do apologise. Yes, it is. I even supplemented some of the letters which were missing in this list. I hope they were at least given a proper burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm very grateful for the Court for allowing us to run through, but it seemed sensible to get through this exercise before we took the break. There's nothing else I need to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is only one more question. Would you like to finish with that? What would you rather do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It will be all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be perhaps preferable to finish with the questions of the Prosecution before the break, because after that, there will be questions from the Defence. But it's up to you. The last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have finished the questioning. He's acknowledged both lists, I think, as marked by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you recognised both the lists, I understand. All right. Now, I think we are going to take a break, and I hope somebody from the Victims and Witnesses Unit will take care of Witness M. We shall take a 30-minute break, I believe. The session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are resuming. Will you bring in the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness M, have you had a good rest? If you wish, you may look at the accused. We may also ask you if you can identify him, but I'm interested in your mental health. Are you all right? Are you better now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was simply the list, because there is a man on the list and he was more than a brother to me when I was a small boy. So I saw it, and I felt terribly distressed at seeing it because I do not know where his bones lie. I do not know where he is. It would mean a great deal to me if I knew where he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we do understand that, of course. Now, will you please focus on the questions that will be asked by the counsel for the Defence? Don't be too distressed. The accused has the right to a defence, whatever you might think. Therefore, his lawyer will now ask you questions. Please focus on these questions and try to be as precise as possible. Mr. Greaves, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. M, can I just start by saying two things to you, please? The first is this: If you don't understand my question, stop me, tell me to do it again. All right? Will you do that for me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second thing is if you feel yourself becoming distressed, please don't worry; just stop, take your time, and I'll keep an eye on you and match your feelings as far as possible. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I've got to ask you some questions and I'll make it as quick as I can for you. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. M, I just want to ask you briefly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphones or could the microphones be brought closer to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think one of the microphones is not on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: My monitor. I have no image on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think one of your microphones keeps going off, and I don't know how that will affect the ability of the interpreters to hear you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Is it all right now? It is. It is now. Yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. M, can you please answer this about yourself: Prior to the war, did you engage in any way in the political life of your community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you -- did you do so either during or have you done so since the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, please, about the day when the bridges over the Sava River were blown. On the day that they were blown, at 7.30 in the morning, did you go to the area and see some of the results of that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It was when I started for work. I turned back, because when you drive a car, that was practically the only way I could take to get to work. At any rate, which was nearer so that I did stop at the bridge for awhile. When I saw all that horror, I almost was sick, but I was in a hurry to get to work, so I really had no time to think about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct: that you were able to see that there had been casualties, both in terms of wounded and killed, as a result of that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to know the detail of how any person had been killed, but what sort of quantity of people had been killed or wounded? Was it hundreds or tens or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I won't go into statistics. I will say what I heard from other people, because that morning two buses had arrived from Vienna, in Austria, with our migrant workers, and only that bridge, because at Orasje the bridge had already been demolished, so that all had to take this Gunja bridge in Brcko. That morning there were a lot of fatalities. It was a matter of hundreds rather than dozens or tens, as you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you now, please, about May the 1st. On that day, I think that soldiers started taking over various public buildings. Did you present yourself and assist in the organisation of patrols in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May and on the 3rd of May I was patrolling in my street. I don't know if I should mention the names of other people I was patrolling the street with. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yet -- I mean, the first day might be ugly until the Serbs took the positions they wanted for themselves, but after they did this everything would go back to normal, as before. So all the neighbourhood communities patrolled the town, because of possible robberies rather than possible entry of Serb forces, because they were already stationed in the barracks around Brcko, but not in Kolobara and not towards the exit from Brcko to the Brka, because that was the majority Muslim population there, so that they flinched away from it or perhaps they had a plan which we knew nothing about. On the 2nd or 3rd of May, we, therefore, had our patrols. I was a part of that on the 2nd and 3rd of May. Those were street patrols or, rather, looking after houses and property of those who had left Bosnia-Herzegovina already. I believe there were about six or seven families, Muslim families, which had left, and that was why we organised that. It was -- it was nothing terrible. We practically were simply trying to protect ourselves against thieves, because at that time cars were stolen on a large scale in Brcko at that time already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct: that the patrols were organised by Papa, and he had been appointed by the SDA to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I cannot say that this is not true. I cannot deny that fact, but I know that he was appointed on behalf of the SDA because he was a member of the party of SDA and he was the most -- how shall I put it? He was the first one in that business. He was appointed by the SDA as the mayor of the neighbourhood community of Kolobara. So this was -- that is, they simply appointed the man to the right place, I suppose, even though I wasn't particularly happy with his appointment to that post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one final question about these patrols. Did he, in fact, provide one of the weapons that were used by the patrols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: During those night patrols, those two night patrols in which I took part -- and I could lose my head because of that, he said -- but I was issued with a hunting rifle, a two-barrelled. That's an older one, the type that was once used for hunting. But at that particular time, it could be used for anything, I mean short of my own shooting of my leg if it went off. I mean it could be used to intimidate perhaps somebody, but never to reject an attack if it happened. It was nothing, really. We usually -- we patrolled in threesomes, and each one of us would have a piece of a weapon which Papa had provided for us. That is true, and that is an incontrovertible fact, and I really don't know who he received those weapons from or where he procured them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness M. I'm going to move on now to the time when you were taken to the clinic. There was one man in particular there who I think came to your attention, the man Mauzer. Was he responsible for organising things at the clinic and interrogating people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. He organised the eviction of civilians from their houses, from their yards, from their shelters, their cellars. The way they did it, they came from the centre of the town across the Brka to the bridge. I don't know whether they forded this small river, this riverlet [sic], the Brka. It was swollen in those days, so you would need a boat to cross it unless you used the bridge. But below the cay, they had already entered in the morning of the 4th of May, but they did not advance towards the health centre because some seven or eight hundred metres from the Zenski Bridge or, rather, the women's bridge, as we call it, from Kolobara, that is, (redacted) -- sorry, I'm trying to give you the right picture of how the land lies there. He was the chief of command, but everybody called him Mauzer because he sort of took pride in this name, and he used to say the civilians should feel privileged, honoured, as he put it, to have Arkan's men with them. Arkan's were there to guard us. They sort of protected us so that nobody would kill us until the interrogation and this whole treatment was over; that is, "Where is your neighbour, where is your brother, where is your uncle, where is your father? Was this, was that? Was your weapon -- what kind of arms did you have? Who did you buy it from?" and so on and so forth. It all came down to provocation, practically, and nothing came out of it. But be that as it may, he headed them, and he was issuing instructions as to how they should work. If -- how we put it -- if he identified somebody who -- if he spotted somebody who was more afraid than others, then he would take him for interrogation first, realising that that person perhaps was not so stable, and that through him he would be able to discover who had weapons or who was smuggling weapons, because there was all sorts of stories circulating about how weapons were smuggled from Croatia. So that would be, for instance, one sign of identification. Then just hitting people. I wasn't hit then, but I saw how he hit my neighbour with the butt of his rifle -- butt of his pistol; not hit very hard; sort of tap him on the head, for instance, with the butt of the pistol. "You're the one, so where is your radio station?" and things like that. I mean that was one of the methods they used, and that was one of the things that I witnessed, and about 100 of my neighbours who were sitting in front of the emergency unit on the pavement with their hands above their head. I already tried to show it to you, but I have problems with my right hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please try to be as concise as possible? Of course, you are telling us some important things, but will you please try to answer the questions to the point, if you can?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness M, if you do it as quickly as possible, of course, you'll be finished more quickly. So if you can remember that. I know you've got things to tell us, but as far as possible, I'm trying to focus your mind on what I'm trying to deal with. All right? Was there an occasion, during your stay at the clinic, when Mauzer and another soldier went to each detainee in turn and asked to examine their hands? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Mauzer had a man with him who was smelling hands, because he said allegedly that that's the way you could tell whether somebody was a sniper or not, because then he could smell oil or gunpowder on his hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, I think the soldier went as far as actually to sniff at the hands. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, myself included; everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst the people in whom Mauzer was interested, was there somebody -- and I don't want to have the name of the person -- was there somebody who was accused of being in possession of a radio transmitter? Don't tell us his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in particular trouble because he was suspected of using the radio and of having caused the deaths of some Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had caused it, to make it clear, because the radio transmissions had interfered with military transmissions? That was the accusation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. Was the focus of their anger because he was alleged to have caused the deaths because his radio had interfered with military radio transmissions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: That's correct, because this was just used as a pretext to beat him, because there was no electricity then and a radio transmitter is electricity run.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help us about this: When you were at the mosque, were the guards there what you describe as Arkan's soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The guards were Arkan's soldiers, whereas Mauzer's men worked at the medical centre. They were shooting from windows at Klanac, where this resistance movement was on the Federal side. Those who had opposed, on the 2nd of May -- or rather on the 1st of May, they offered resistance. The situation changed a bit on the 2nd. But there was a kind of conflict in which even the Yugoslav air force fired against these positions. At the medical centre, they were shooting from the windows, and they kept us as a human shield. I was part of that human shield. I had to clean the broken glass so that they could kneel and shoot properly, and if I did not stand straight enough, they would hit me so that I would be a living target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that fighting, were there casualties, both from firearms or from artillery or bombing runs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The artillery did not fire, there was no bombing, but I think light arms were used. I don't know. I don't know. I just saw them flying over, but on that day no bombs were thrown. Over there, I mean the place that I spoke of, Klanac, there were no bombs from aircraft that day. There was street fighting. Mauzer's men put a tank between the main building and the post office, and the tank was facing Klanac, and they used the tank to shoot with light arms, mostly snipers, as well as heavier arms. The man who was sniffing at our fingers, he climbed up on the mosque, and he was shooting from the mosque at Klanac. Sorry. I hit the desk now. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I had digressed slightly because I had wanted to ask about that and I had forgotten. Just returning to the mosque, did you overhear or hear one of the soldiers there saying something along these lines: that you would not be hurt if you were not guilty of anything and would be released if there were no problems? Do you recall hearing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: (redacted). I also did other things. Quite a few Muslims from the area of Leman were killed for no reason whatsoever, just because they were Muslims, and a young man recognised me at the health centre. He went to school with my sister. He tried to make things as easy as possible for me. It could not have been easy, because they would hit us in passing whenever they could. So he could not help me altogether when I was being interrogated by Mauzer's men, but this captain who was in front of the mosque with us, he was in charge of the military. He was not in charge of civilians at all, but he was considerate towards the elderly and towards children and towards the sickly. So he defended me at a given point in time, so I am really grateful for that. Not everybody should be condemned for certain things. Not everybody is guilty for those things. I condemn what was done, not a man as a man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. If I can just draw you back to the focus of my question. One of the soldiers, it's right, isn't it, whilst you were at the mosque -- and this may well have been someone who was aware of you or something -- said you wouldn't be hurt if you were not guilty of anything, that you would be released if there were no problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand from the phrase "not guilty of anything"? What did you understand that to mean in the context of the way it was said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: If I did not have any contact with weapons, as such, that is to say the procurement of weapons, the buying or selling of weapons, if I was not in the SDA party, then I could have been at peace and I didn't have to worry about anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. M. From the mosque, a number of detainees were taken for interrogation at the clinic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, do you recall them interrogating the man who had the radio? Again, don't tell us his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst they were interrogating him about the signals he'd passed and the codes that he's used and the organisation he was working for, whilst that was going on was he being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that the focus of that beating was the fact that he had -- that they suspected that he had been involved in some form of communication with the resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was another man sitting next to you. Again, I don't want to repeat his name. He was writing out a list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you could tell, was that names of people who were SDA party members and people who had weapons and people who were involved in the supply of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Quite possible, and it's quite logical. The young man was born there and he knew everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were interrogated, Mr. M, again, was the focus of that interrogation -- put aside for the moment anything that was done to you, but the questions, did they focus again on the issue of weapons, the SDA, and who was organising resistance, and topics of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, did you yourself come under suspicion for having been involved in the blowing up of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just refresh your memory. I think you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995 and a statement was drawn up but you never signed it. Is that correct? That's a document you've been taken through in the last couple days or so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a captain, I think, interrogating you, and at one point he pushed a soldier away and suggested there was a description of someone who was involved in blowing up the bridge, a description which you fitted. Does that refresh your memory about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: That wasn't written out properly. I did not say that I was personally being blamed for it. All those who had longish hair and who were skinny were candidates, so to speak. But they were aware of the fact that they had done it; they had blown up the bridge, not anyone from the Croatian side or the Muslim side. It was just used as a pretext for beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, please, about the last time that you saw Papa and three brothers called Terzic, who, I think, had been interrogated at the clinic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I recall that. When I was a living target, when I was cleaning up glass, they made all three of us go into that room. I think Redzep Sakic or Senad was with me at the time. I don't know exactly anymore, but at any rate, they were making Muhamed Terzic, one of the three brothers, to jump on his chest from a table that was this high [indicates]. Papa was laying on the floor, and they made this man to jump from the table onto Papa's chest. They forced him to do it. They forced him at gunpoint. They put a knife and a gun, they put on his chin, and they made him do it. This man was crying and he said, "Oh, but I can't do it," and the other man was in a terrible state. He was all bloody and ripped up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you all right? Do you want a moment? Just pause for a moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If I can just help you with this. During this incident, were some rifles or some weapons brought in, apparently from Papa's house, and was one of those weapons one of the ones that you'd had on patrol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: All rifles, all hunting guns are the same. I had not really known anything about rifles until then. I only had one rifle that I used while doing my military service. So I probably would not have recognised the rifle that I had on duty, because I didn't carry it around all the time because we took two-hour shifts. It's not that we had weapons throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But can you confirm they brought in the weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, they brought in the weapons, but probably it wasn't those weapons. I mean, maybe they could have been those weapons, because the young man who was writing things down on the bench, he was with us on these night-duty shifts, but then -- I don't know. I can't say for sure. I can only tell you what I know for sure, one hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now briefly to your detention at the Luka facility. Was it your recollection that at one stage during the day, the 8th of May, Goran Jelisic apparently said something along the following lines: that you were to be questioned, that those who were not guilty should not worry, that those who were clean and not extremists will get passes and be freed, and that they were going to find the snipers amongst you? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Possible snipers, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Possible snipers. And as to the rest of it, that's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The word "clean," what did you understand the word "clean" to mean in the context of what was being said to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Well, it depends in what context you're using that word. "Clean" can mean cleaning a floor, and "clean" can mean cleaning a window, and it is well-known fact what "cleansing" by the Serb people meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This wasn't cleansing in that context. Would this be right: that what it referred to was if you're not involved in the SDA, if you're not in the resistance, you're not extremists, you're not snipers, then you've got nothing to worry about? Would that be a fair summary of what it meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Well, listen, I imagine that would suit someone, but you should be aware of one thing, that quite a few killings occurred. And if anyone told a Bosnian orthodox person that he was a thief or if he quarrelled at the football game or if they had a fight while they were drunk, that was -- that was sufficient for him to be killed. He'd be called a murderer, a sniper, whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help me about this, please, Mr. M: During the course of the day, the 8th of May, would it be right that there were large numbers of people both coming into the Luka facility and leaving it? By that I mean detainees rather than military personnel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking about hundreds coming in and hundreds going out? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so. You must bear in mind the fear, all that fear that weighed upon us. So I don't really think that anyone exaggerated. I think these figures are realistic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You yourself were released later that day. Were you released alone or in a large group of people? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Well, I was among the last to receive a pass for my life, around 8.30. At 9.00 there was a curfew, and we had a maximum 15 to 20 minutes to find a safe place to be in, or otherwise, we would end up at the SUP again, or Posavina, that was also full of civilians, or at the nuclear shelter, or again back at Luka. As a matter of fact, I was told I should not go to Kolobara because those who were coming from the front line could even kill me. Who did not know me could see that I was a Muslim and could kill me. That is what I was told by a man. I think he knows Goran very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to complete that part, were you part of a group that was released, as I asked, or did you get released alone? A group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No. I was in a group that numbered about 70 people, perhaps up to 100, because all of us stood by the hangar, from the beginning of the hangar, so to speak, to the middle, because the hangar is about 100 metres long, perhaps less, a bit less. So say there was a 50-metre line of us, two by two. So there were about 100 of us who were supposed to be released, but I cannot give the exact figure. I told you that we all had to keep our heads bowed down. It depends who behaved in what way. Some people came and let the minors clean firearms. All of them were thieves, and they were shooting in the streets, and they tried to see who was a better marksman, who could hit a person who was moving and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. M, I want to ask you now about this, please: When you were subsequently -- just give me a moment, please -- released from detention completely in 1992, did you have an interview with the security services in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. If possible, could I say something before you do about this interview, with your permission, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Please tell us what you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yesterday or, rather, today, today I had a look at the list and I'm not satisfied with it. I gave that list in November 1992 or, rather, this interview, this paper, and some of my words were changed. I personally was never, well, ethnically conscious, so to speak. I don't know if you've heard of the notion of fraternity and unity. That's the way I was brought up. So although I went through all these horrors and terrors and tortures and camps, I did not look upon all in the same way. However, there were some people who took this down and corrected some things. It's not the way I put. You know, the words that are used there, "Chetniks," whatever. There weren't many Chetniks; two or three. They called themselves Vojvodas. Goran Jelisic said that he was the "Serb Adolf." If he considers himself that, well and fine, it's for him to say, but those are not the words that I used. But I signed this probably because I was fed up. I'm sorry if someone is offended by what I just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. M. It's very helpful, and I may just ask you one or two more questions about it. You've been through that document here in The Hague, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Today. Today, I saw it today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of the statement, did you append your signature to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I did, but this statement was read out to me by a person, and I just glanced at it and signed it. Sorry. The statement that I gave and that was of great strategic importance, because I knew where the heavy howitzers were, those that were facing the free territory where they were only civilians, where there were no military men or military facilities, well, that statement's not there. Later on, I was so sorry that that hadn't reached this place too. For me, that was the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this right: that the conclusion of the statement that you made to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities says this: "At the end, I declare that I quoted my personal observations and that everything I said conforms to facts which I certificate with my autograph." I think that means signature. "I'm prepared to repeat everything I said here in court or before any international organisation which might be interested in the matter." Do you remember that as being the final paragraph in the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I think that that is partly all right, but I do not recall all the details that you just mentioned. After all, quite a few years have gone by, and I have experienced so many things that I cannot really recall every little detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, and I've read it out just to remind you of the detail of it, rather than asking you if you can specifically remember having done that. The first thing I want to ask you is this,

utterances.speaker: MR. M
utterances.text: You've told us in evidence today about a number of things which Mr. Jelisic was supposed to have done, and in particular, introducing himself at Luka as "Adolf," about him talking about the cleansing of Muslims, and of Ranko Cesic inviting him to see how he was shooting. You do not mention any of those incidents or remarks in the statement you made a few months after you were released. Can you explain why it is that you didn't say anything about those statements at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: In '92 I recorded a tape or, rather, our television made an interview with me, and it was quite a complete testimony, as this one here, with all the detail, perhaps even more so, but that one was for the state security. It meant nothing to me. I never relied on it. It was only after I gave it to the United Nations, when I was interviewed in Tuzla, it was only then that I went back to a passage in my life. I was simply trying not to live with it anymore. My life started again in November '92 when I came out. I wanted to come here to make certain things clear for myself, to come to terms with myself, because I was also damaged. I suffered many other damages. A lot of my family perished, only because they were Muslims, and could I not choose who my parents would be, whether it be a Serb, a Muslim, or a Croat, whoever. So will you please bear that in mind? I'd really like you, if possible, not to rely on that document that you have before you. It will be best to tear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think you can say that to the counsel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You cannot say that to the counsel for the Defence. He has to do his job. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I do apologise. I do apologise, but at a given moment they asked from me something that could simply be a boost to them, which could provide a different picture, even worse than the one that was really happening. That's what they wanted, and I'd rather say something which is. Some people found it worse in the camp when they were shaved to the skin. What was worse for me was when they made me defecate by the body of a dead man. Different things happened and perceptions are also different. So let's leave that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to another subject, Mr. M. The Zahirovic brothers, you saw both of them being shot? You saw the shots being fired at them, both men being killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you tell the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities this: In relation to one of the brothers you said: "I could see them beating the Zahirovic brother who was between the sidewalk and the road, but I could not see the other one because he was near the hangar, out of my sight. So I watched them beating some two minutes the brother who was between the sidewalk and the road. I later heard three gunshots, and although I didn't see it, I suppose 'Adolf' killed the other brother which was leaning against the hangar, crying and screaming in pain, and after those gunshots there was no more crying." You then describe the second brother being killed with three bullets. Why did you say that to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities, Mr. M?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: You have to understand one thing. I spent eight months in the camp, and I went through a certain crisis when I forget -- when I began to forget the names of my family, of my relatives. Well, not my mother's and my sisters' but say my cousin's name. I simply forgot it. It took me 24 hours for me to remember it. I thought I was going crazy. At some point I weighed only 48 kilograms, because they'd broken my jaw and I couldn't eat. When I went to see a doctor, they said that they would take all my blood and then throw me into the dump -- into the dump yard with all the other corpses. So I'm just beginning to recover.
