The more I dream, the more things begin to repeat. Nightmares I have are beyond description. Sometimes after I have one of those nightmares, it takes me three or four days to fall asleep again. You simply cannot understand that. So I'm saying that statement which I gave immediately after I came out, I go by my statement which I gave to the United Nations when they interviewed me in Tuzla for over three hours. I think it was worse than going through another hell. This one is the third or the fourth time I'm going through a hell, and really, I came here to say what I saw. Yours, of course, is to question me and mine is to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. M, I'm not, therefore, in view of what you said, although I don't necessarily accept it, I'm not going to go into any more detail about your statement to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities. I would like to turn now, please, to something which caused you some distress earlier, and I just ask that we can go into private session, please, in connection with the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Private session, can we, registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand from Mr. Registrar we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We are now back in public session, so, Mr. Nice, you now have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions, and they won't be very long, Witness M. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first question: Papa, you said that you weren't particularly happy with his appointment. It may not matter, but just in one sentence, if you can, why weren't you happy with his appointment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Because (redacted) (redacted) I knew what kind of a burden this is, what kind of a responsibility that is. And a neighbourhood community is even more important, particularly at times like that when one could already glean that something was looming ahead like Bijeljina or something, and I did not think that he was the best person to occupy that post. Had he been more adequate politically, he would have informed his people in time about what was going on, and then those who thought they should stay there would have stayed, and others would have left and thus be saved. He was a victim of his own politics that first day, but unfortunately he took another ten also people with him. You had other witnesses from whom you could hear about him, because many people knew who Papa was. Of course, I am sorry for him as a man, but I did not approve of what he did. If he had some weapons, then he should have either defended at that moment -- he should have either defended his neighbourhood community or just turned in the weapons and not allow that these weapons be found on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of Muslims from a location beginning with "L". I can't remember the exact spelling of the name, but you spoke of some Muslims from that location whom you said were killed just because they were Muslims. Can you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You spoke of witnesses from a particular location who you said, in your evidence, were killed just because they were Muslims. We'll find the location, if necessary, and if you can't remember that piece of evidence, I'll come back to that. But you spoke of Muslims being killed just because they were Muslims. Can you remember the example you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, perhaps it was a long time ago when this question was answered. Perhaps you could help him by referring to the transcript, or I'll ask you to move on to another question and then come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly, you were asked about the apparent criterion or test for selection in Luka camp that was spoken of by a soldier on your arrival; extremists, and passes for those who weren't, and so on. But can you just tell us this: When groups of men were selected to move bodies, were they selected at random or were they selected according to some questioning technique?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, they did not apply any technique. It was simply, "You and you and you," as soon as they would enter the hangar. They wouldn't even look into faces. They would just point at two or three. For a while they were asking for volunteers, but since nobody volunteered, that's what they did. At such moments, if two would go, then one of them would come back, or sometimes none of them would come back. At times, seldom one would come back, but two, I don't think, ever returned, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: (redacted), and what I said is quite enough, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Those who did not return, to your knowledge, had not been identified by any test or criterion to be killed; they were simply people killed at random?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Random, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've now found the name, and indeed it matches my note, but I didn't believe it. Is there a location called Leman, something like Leman or Lemon? L-E-H-M-A-N is the way it's spelled in the transcript. What you said was, "Quite a few Muslims from the area of Leman were killed for no reason whatsoever, just because they were Muslims." Then you went on at this part of your evidence to say, "And a young man recognised me at the health centre." This was in a passage of your evidence where you had just spoken of (redacted), so if the transcript has got the location incorrectly recorded, that might help you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. Perhaps it's because I'm so upset today, I can't really concentrate, and I cannot even recall. I don't know. I don't know, honestly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I shan't take you any further on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Most probably, it was the kind of mistake like the one that I had to correct in that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked questions about suspicion of blowing up the bridge. So far as you were aware, from your discussions with others at the time, were the Muslims in any way responsible for blowing up that bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, not really. At first, the Serb Radio Brcko had made its first announcements by the barracks, and it is from the barracks that they set out to take the radio station, the medical centre, the medical emergency centre, the PTT post office. I'm sorry, I'm really so upset I simply can't concentrate. Could you just put your question once again, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was whether, from your discussions, there was any truth in any suggestion that the Muslims had had anything to do with blowing up that bridge. Who was responsible, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now I know. They did not say that the Muslims had blown up the bridge, because it was well known that they had done it. There was a patrol of ours that was guarding the bridge, and Jasko, an active policeman, was at the bridge, and he was taken away at around 3.00. I saw him after I was released from the camp. He told me himself that a special unit, members came from Belgrade, and he said we were told to go home, to do whatever we wanted to do, to go home and to "let us take over", so they are the ones who did this. And what -- they just wanted to beat someone up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, any suggestion that you or any other Muslim was involved in the blowing up of the bridge, was that, in your judgement, a genuine allegation or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, no. It was just make-believe. "Yes, you fit the description. We're going to beat you, and then we're going to ask you something else. And if you can take more of it, then we're going to beat you some more."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two more questions only. The first relates to what you were asked about your sightings of the killings at the grate, and I'm only asking this question, as the Court will understand that I'm not sure whether the killings by Jelisic are admitted or not. Just help us, please. When you came into court today, did you think you would be able to identify the person you saw doing those killings if you were to see him here today or not? Do you have a view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Believe me, I didn't think about it at all, nor do I need that. You know what? The man who was supposed to kill you actually released you. From the moment I got into Luka, I was supposed to be the fourth or the fifth person. Perhaps I'm going to be haunted by that. Perhaps all these nightmares will finally be over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to take you back, though, to the question. Did you think you'd be able to identify the person if you were to see him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I told you that I did not think about it at all. That would only be an additional burden for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the event having been in this courtroom, have you been able to identify the person who you saw doing the killings or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the person who killed both the brothers and the other man who had to lick his hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last question, Witness M, relates to what you said, I think twice now, about people being left alive and then being used for the exchange of prisoners. Was this something that was explained as a policy, or was this something that people discussed or guessed about or worked out? Help us, if you will, with how you offer that as an explanation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: When I came -- I don't know exactly which date this was in May, it's so hard for me to concentrate, but when I came to Luka, Kosta, Kole -- I know him personally, but I can't remember his last name -- he was in charge of the Luka camp then. He was head of the camp. He was surprised how come I was there, how come that I hadn't escaped someplace. I was, in a way, protected by him. We were together in Banja [phoen] and Gradacac. He had a problem. He was a house painter, but he fell off the ladder and broke his leg or something, and I had problems with my back, so we were in this spot together. He told me that there was no reason for me to be afraid, that it wasn't the 8th or the 15th or the 1st of May, that from the 15th onwards the systematic killing had stopped and that now all were being kept alive for all. That's how he had put it. There was supposed to be some kind of an exchange across the Sava River and he put me on that list for an exchange. However, nothing came out of this exchange because they couldn't reach agreement on it ultimately. So most of the information I had I got precisely from those people who kept us detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information about exchange coming from them, did they --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- explain where they heard it from, how high up in the line of authority they heard this information from, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Well, probably -- I think that it was someone from their command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the difference between guessing and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Because they started viewing us as civilians. I'm sure of what I'm saying. My assessment of the situation never brought me into trouble, so I stand by what I say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other questions in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nice. I shall now turn to my colleagues. Judge Riad has a question, I believe. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. Witness M -- I can't call you by your name, so I just say good afternoon, Witness M. If it is no strain for you, you can just talk, and you can just help me understand perhaps some of your assertions or declarations, if you can help me see it more clearly. You mentioned that just as a matter of course and of fact, that it is known what cleansing by the Serbian people meant. It is known what cleansing by the Serbian people meant. What is "known"? Can you just tell us this in your words? It's a very jealous [phoen] statement and very important.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Well, I understand myself when I'm talking, but you probably have a bit of difficulty in understanding what I'm saying. It so happened that the president of the Republic of Serbia, the ex-Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic, wanted to make a Greater Serbia out of all ex-Yugoslavia. He didn't succeed in doing that, so he wanted to do it at least by taking half of Bosnia, attaching it to Serbia and turning it into a Greater Serbia. So that's what I refer to when I said cleansing the others by the Serbs. They would kill part, and the remainder would be used as slaves, and the rest would be expelled. You can find that in documents that were available to the public. I saw this on CNN. I watched this on television. After all, this is not a public secret. I mean, it's no secret. It's a factual state, because that is why Serbia was bombed by NATO. I'm sorry to be reacting in this way but, you know, when they started bombing them, I felt as if I were bombing them, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. But the CNN is not one of our sources. You are our source, so you have to tell us what is your first-hand experience.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I just said what you have available to you, especially this kind of testimony. You have a victim, a victim who was a victim and still is a victim and hopefully will stop being a victim, but there are a lot of people who cannot get rid of this burden, people who even die from -- die and still bear it. I know a lot of people who committed suicide on the free territory after the camp because they couldn't live with it any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to hear that. You also mentioned, as a matter of fact, that there was some kind of selective murder. You called it selective murder. When there is a selective murder, what is -- "selection" means that there is a basis for the selection. Was a basis for this selective matter? You said that they were all civilians. So what was the basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I'm very glad that you took me back to this in order to clarify it to you. It so happened that three days before the bridges would be blown up I went to the SDA club to (redacted) (redacted), because that is one of the things I did inter alia. Later on, when I heard what had happened to our people, I saw this document that was at Klanac, and that is practically why the war had started before the Serbs were supposed actually to attack us. And there was a list, and at the very top of this chapter it said all people who had university degrees, who were doctors, teachers, professors, directors -- do you understand what I mean -- all of these who held these high positions, they were selectively killed. It was no longer a question whether he was a member of the SDA or not. He was simply supposed to be killed. Those were the ones who were killed during this first wave, and this first wave involved such a great number of casualties that it is simply inconceivable. And these three lists that I react to so emotionally, I feel like dying when I have a look at them. I feel awful. It hurts so bad. But there is this list that I can only guarantee to you that is ten times longer; not only for Brcko, but all of Bosnia; not ten times longer, but a hundred times longer. Our people still don't know where these people are, because they're not in other states and they're not there, and after all this first selection, I mean, to go back to that now, so that is this first selection of the most highly educated, then the richest. I know what was done. I can go on about this endlessly. That is not the point. The point is for you to understand what they did to us. The third thing was simply looting. When they had nothing else to loot -- I mean, the lowliest population, but there wasn't anybody who was really lowly. I mean, everybody had a job. Whoever wanted to work could have a job. I had three jobs; one, two, three. I was a universal man. But that's not the point. The point is that it was only Muslims. Look, Goran Jelisic is not the one and only. There are quite a few Goran Jelisics, but I only know him. Look at statistics. Look at how many people were killed in Brcko in addition to the things that he was involved in. But that's not that Goran Jelisic, and it's not only one Hitler. There are many other Hitlers, small Hitlers. But that wasn't the problem. The problem is if you're a Muslim and if they are afraid of you, then they have to eliminate you one way or the other. They're either going to terrify you and you're going to flee to a third country on your own, or you're going to stay there and they're going to exterminate you somehow. So that is this selection. That is this selective treatment of Muslims. To tell you the truth, what they did to us they portrayed as if we were doing it to them. They were talking about some kind of list that we had made that Serbs were supposed to be slaughtered, et cetera, also that Alija Izetbegovic did not want to take us when they would exchange us. I mean, they were simply trying to evade the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We're going out of the real question. Start from the top and going down. Start from the top, the people representing the society, the people who had power in their hand, the money in their hand; is that right? And the method was mainly to exterminate or to transfer, because you said cleansing included many things. You are apparently well informed. So was it mainly exterminating or just inviting them to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: That's the way it turned out, that it was a kind of ethnic cleansing that later gained great momentum, and then they practically remained on their own. When they had no one else to loot, then they started looting themselves. So you have to bear that in mind. Sorry that I'm speaking this way, but I hope that you understand what I'm trying to say. They simply wanted to be on their own as a nation. They didn't want to have any Muslims, they didn't want to have any Croats around. However, it's easier to reach agreement with the Croats because the Croats have a country of their own too, and we bother them. If necessary, they would buy that part of Bosnia that belongs to them and then they would remain on their own. Do you see what my point is? That is what ethnic cleansing means. I'm sorry if you didn't understand my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I did. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Rodrigues? Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness M, good afternoon. I should like to go back to this matter of selection and to look at it from another angle. I should like to ask you what was the ethnicity of people who were detained or kept in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: That is a question that I expected from the very outset. It was put, but perhaps I didn't clarify things sufficiently. At the mosque, most of the people were Muslims. The majority were Muslims. If there were any Croats, perhaps there were two, three, or four of them, because they were immediately separated from us and they were taken to the military barracks. From the military barracks, they went to free territory, or to Croatia, or someplace, or they were kept for exchanges. I don't want anybody to be offended by this. I was told by Kosta, Kole, that their price was high, that they were worth more because they could get more for one of them. So the point was they could do whatever they wanted to us. So let me tell you, the worst thing that could happen to me -- perhaps I'm speaking at great length -- but they made us relieve ourselves in the mosque. I cannot forgive these leaders for that, this person Mauzer. I think that even animals would not do that worst thing. I mean, if you can house-train a cat -- I'm sorry. I'm begging your pardon, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in the mosque, the majority were Muslim and there were three or four Croats. How about the barracks? What was the ethnicity of people who were taken to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Your Honour, all these Croats were already warned on time, either by the Serbs or the Croats from Croatian. Very few of them had remained. If they did stay back, they stayed on their own, because if somebody had told me what was in the making and if I had someplace to go, I probably would have gone. But very, very few of them remained. A surprisingly small number remained at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now the same question but as regards Luka. How about Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: The same. I would say that there were very few of them, as many as fingers on one hand. When they asked whether there were any volunteers for the Serb army, one of the Croats volunteered, and he joined the artillery because he was an artilleryman while doing his military service, I imagine, so he went. There weren't very many of them. Five or six. I'm sorry. In my hangar where I was, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Right. My last question with which I'm trying to get the whole picture, were there more Croats in the mosque or at Luka? Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: There were fewer Croats at the mosque. If you're talking about the percentage, I think it is more or less the same, but in terms of actual numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I really want to know if this idea of selection was applied at different stages in the -- from the beginning to their ending up at Luka. It seems, from your evidence, that they took everybody from the mosque, or almost everybody, and after that a selection took place. I don't know if I'm right or not, but you have answered my questions. But if we take the same persons in the beginning, was there a selection? Did a selected number or group of people reach Luka or later on? Luka, I guess, was worse than the mosque. So it was mostly this general question, whether in practice one could really follow this selection.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: Yes. You see, there are four or five improvised camps where people were brought together, and they were so crowded that they couldn't even sit. They had to stand by one another. That was the Posavina Hotel. I said it was the nuclear shelter. Then Partizan, the gym Partizan in Brcko; then Laser, the transportation company, the bus company, you know; then -- I can't remember the name, but Bimeks. It was a Bimeks outlet, a farm or something. At the farm, yes, there was a complex there, and that is where the hospital was for the wounded Serbs. On the other side, there were detainees, Muslims and Croats. Luka was the main centre for executions and for releases; that is to say that everybody came to Luka. Some of them were sent back. It depends. For example, two or three buses would come per day. Fortunately, I was there only for one day, but some people, who unfortunately were there from the beginning of May until the 24th or 25th when we were taken to Batkovic, I can just tell about things I heard, and that's only logical. In Luka -- in Luka, it was the last stop. Luka was the last stop. Either you would get executed or you would be transferred to, say, Batkovic, as happened to me. Also, there was selection. I mean names were called out in Luka, because they did not know what the exact number was and then they counted everybody, and I don't know what all. So for example, they'd be looking for a man and they'd start -- they'd -- they could not find him because perhaps they mispronounced his name or surname. Later on, when they would realise that there was a mispronunciation involved, when they would finally find him, then they'd beat him even worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To conclude, after your description, could one say that one could find Croats at the mosque but it was very difficult to find Croats in Luka? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. There were Croats in Luka. However, there were quite a few of us. In my opinion, though, in my hangar there were three, four, to five persons, but they left quickly. Either a friend, a Serb friend, would come to get them out or they'd simply leave. Hardly any of them were killed, although some were killed. For example, they wouldn't want to take a man to the camp or anywhere, they'd simply go to his home and kill him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you, Witness M.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. Right. I believe this is the end. Did you speak freely? Did you tell us all you wanted? You said that you could talk until tomorrow. We do understand that, but you answered questions. Is there something you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M
utterances.text: I would like to thank you for being so considerate and for allowing me to say more than you asked me to say. However, I was so upset today, and I think I've relaxed a bit by now. Perhaps I'm a bit more stable now. I don't know how to put it. I wanted to portray all of this for you, but it's not possible. It is different for listeners and it is different for the actual players who were involved. It's like at a football game. You can be there as a fan, but it's different when you're actually running around and playing football. As for me, I am not anyone's judge. I don't condemn Goran Jelisic. I condemn the things he did. If he is guilty, it is a well-known fact who he will be held accountable by; God first and then you. If he can sleep peacefully, then that is his own affair. I do not -- I cannot sleep peacefully and I haven't touched anyone. I thank you, at any rate, and I thank this entire organisation. I hope that in this way, I managed to get some things away from me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And that you, who did not put your finger on anyone, that you will find the peace that you deserve, evidently. Will you please stay here for a while? It is now quarter to 6.00. Mr. Nice, is the next witness here? Would you start him today or would you rather that we begin tomorrow, that he begins to give his evidence tomorrow? We shall perhaps have two or three days next week. How do you think we should now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is here. He's a protected witness, and he's to be taken by Mr. Tochilovsky. We are, of course, content to start him this evening, and we are in the Chamber's hands. Maybe ten minutes is the maximum we would achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a matter I want to raise that rises out of the re-examination of the witness. It is a point raised by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps we shall tell the witness that his testimony's finished. I do not think there is time to call the next witness. I believe the interpreters are tired too, and if we're going to have a debate now, perhaps we'll have to yet make another break. Mr. Greaves, you know that you do not have the right to re-examine. There is a principal, there is the right of answer, and then Judges ask their questions, and that is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I didn't want to ask any questions. I want to raise a matter that's been raised before, and I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Right. Yes. All right. All right. Yes, but shall we wait for the witness to leave, please? Witness M, thank you very much. You'll now be escorted from the courtroom with all the protective measures as due.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you once again. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Greaves. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During his re-examination, my learned friend made an observation, which was more comment than anything, about the killings at the grate. Can I remind Your Honour of the agreed factual basis for the guilty pleas to be entered by Goran Jelisic, a document which was created at the request of the learned Judge, Judge Riad, which says in respect of the killings of Huso and Smajl Zahirovic, as follows: Counts 20 to 21, which refers to the number, in fact, given to the second indictment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course. I'm sorry. Reads as follows: "Goran Jelisic will plead guilty to Counts 20 and 21 and admit that on or about the 8th of May, 1992, he took two Muslim brothers, Huso and Smajl Zahirovic, outside the main hangar at Luka camp and shot and killed one of them." That is a document that is signed by the Prosecution and Defence. There is more. In the second amended indictment, that killing has now been altered to Count 16 and 17, and the actual indictment reads as follows: "On or about the 8th of May, 1992, at Luka camp, Goran Jelisic took two Muslim brothers from Zvornik ..." and names them: "... outside of the main hangar building where he shot and killed one of them." That's an agreed state of affairs as between the Prosecution and the Defence. This witness claimed to have seen both of them. It is for that reason that I challenged him as to his ability to properly recall the details of that matter, and it's for that reason that I cross-examined the witness in that way. Your Honour, what I'm concerned about is that the Prosecution is allowed to re-examine witnesses on the basis which seems to be, on the face of it, one they do not adhere to themselves if this document is to be accepted by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I believe that I've already said that the witness is not here, so he cannot repeat. But he tried to show, for the Prosecution, and when he turned to the Defence, to answer to you, and he was testifying here about the crime of genocide. Yes, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have nothing very much to say by way of answer, save this: There is a difference between those killings that are charged as specific counts in the indictment and other killings which are relied upon for the case generally and the particular count of genocide that you are trying. The agreement that he killed one brother as the base of a particular count in the indictment doesn't exclude his direct or indirect culpability for the killing of the other brother, and at the end of the evidence, you will have all the evidence from all the witnesses, and you will either find, in relation to that other brother, that he killed him directly himself, therefore it is additional to that which is the subject of the indictment as a specific count, or you'll find that he didn't, or you'll find he was a participant through the hands of someone else. But the questions that I asked are nevertheless correctly asked when the whole basis of the evidence that he gives is being tested. His evidence was, and it will be for you to judge his evidence, that he saw Jelisic kill both of them. If that is the evidence and it's good evidence, then it's evidence that I'm entitled to explore. I'm not seeking to undue any agreement, but there is no agreement that he didn't kill the other brother. I'm just checking with Mr. Tochilovsky, who was, of course, present at those agreements when I wasn't, to make sure I understood them correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing further to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I believe the Judges have nothing to add to this. Mr. Greaves believed that the Judges have nothing to say. Your observations are on the record. I shall repeat that we are here to judge Goran Jelisic for his responsibility for the genocide. Right. But now we shall be able to give a five-minute break which we took away from the interpreters. Now we will have it, because we are five minutes early today. We shall resume tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.55 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of September, 1999, at 10.00 a.m. 25
